title: 3-Read Friday #116
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's weekly 3-Read Friday digest (#116) curates and frames three education blog posts. First, Daisy Christodoulou pushes back on the promise that AI will finally 'personalise' learning, arguing that building lessons around student interests — teaching equations 'through the medium of Taylor Swift' — fundamentally misunderstands how analogies work, because the link to prior knowledge has to fit the content, not the learner's hobby. Second, Robert Pondiscio asks why the knowledge-rich curriculum keeps losing in practice even though the evidence war is won — cognitive science, the science of reading, and even AI all confirm it — and offers 19 reasons it stalls at implementation. Third, Becky Allen argues that teachers keep arguing about how to introduce negative numbers or fractions not because the profession is muddled but because these first-encounter lessons are where sound instructional principles collide and expert judgement is required.
points: Article 1 (Daisy Christodoulou): personalising lessons around student interests misunderstands how analogies work — the link to prior knowledge must fit the content, not the learner's hobby.
Christodoulou's 'Taylor Swift' example illustrates the category error at the heart of interest-based AI personalisation.

Article 2 (Robert Pondiscio): the evidence war over knowledge-rich curriculum is won — cognitive science, the science of reading, and AI all confirm it — yet it keeps losing in practice, for 19 reasons.
Article 3 (Becky Allen): persistent disagreements over teaching fractions or negative numbers mark the 'first-encounter' lessons where sound instructional principles collide.
Barton frames all three as a coherent set about the limits of personalisation, the gap between evidence and implementation, and the need for expert teacher judgement.

Allen argues that teachers keep arguing about how to introduce negative numbers or fractions not because the profession is muddled, but because these first-encounter lessons are where sound instructional principles collide.
The promise that AI will finally “personalise” learning is everywhere right now, so I loved reading a proper, evidence-grounded pushback.
It’s written about American schools, but every one of these obstacles will feel familiar to anyone who’s championed a knowledge-rich curriculum over here.
